claim: Semiconductor production is commonly divided into three segments: design, manufacturing (wafer fabrication), and assembly, testing and packaging (ATP).
evidence: "Semiconductor production includes three segments: (1) design, (2) manufacturing, and (3) assembly, testing, and packaging (ATP)." (CSET, pp. 3-4); "Three broad steps are involved in the production of semiconductors: (1) design; (2) manufacturing; and (3) assembly, testing, and packaging" (GAO-22-105923, p. 4)

claim: In front-end manufacturing, specialized facilities called fabs print nanometer-scale integrated circuits from the chip design into silicon wafers.
evidence: "Highly specialized semiconductor manufacturing facilities, typically called 'fabs', print the nanometer-scale integrated circuits from the chip design into silicon wafers" (BCG/SIA 2021, p. 16)

claim: The back-end stage converts the silicon wafers produced by fabs into finished chips ready to be assembled into electronic devices.
evidence: "This stage involves converting the silicon wafers produced by the fabs into finished chips that are ready to be assembled into electronic devices" (BCG/SIA 2021, p. 19)

claim: Depending on the product, wafer manufacturing involves roughly 400 to 1,400 process steps.
evidence: "Depending on the specific product, there are 400 to 1,400 steps in the overall manufacturing process [of] semiconductor wafers" (BCG/SIA 2021, p. 16)

claim: The average time to fabricate finished semiconductor wafers (cycle time) is about 12 weeks.
evidence: "The average time to fabricate finished semiconductor wafers, known as the cycle time, is about 12 weeks" (BCG/SIA 2021, p. 16)

metric.name: Average wafer fabrication cycle time
metric.population: Front-end wafer fabrication only (excludes design and back-end)

claim: ASML states that the microchip manufacturing process involves hundreds of steps and can take up to four months from design to mass production.
evidence: "The microchip manufacturing process involves hundreds of steps and can take up to four months from design to mass production." (ASML, How microchips are made)

metric.name: Time from design to mass production (upper bound)
metric.population: Microchips generally; scope of 'design to mass production' not defined

claim: Modern chips can have up to 100 layers, all of which must align on top of each other with nanometer precision.
evidence: "Modern chips can have up to 100 layers, which all need to align on top of each other with nanometer precision" (ASML, How microchips are made)

metric.name: Maximum layer count of a modern chip

claim: Silicon wafers are sliced from a highly purified silicon bar called an ingot and polished to extreme smoothness.
evidence: "Wafers are sliced from a salami-shaped bar of 99.99% pure silicon (known as an 'ingot') and polished to extreme smoothness." (ASML, Six crucial steps)

claim: Chipmaking repeats a loop of deposition, photoresist coating, lithography, etching and ion implantation, and a chip goes through this process hundreds of times.
evidence: "Thin films of conducting, isolating or semiconducting materials ... are deposited on the wafer"; "The wafer is then covered with a light-sensitive coating called 'photoresist'"; "the wafer may be bombarded with positive or negative ions"; "each microchip goes through this process hundreds of times before it becomes part of a device." (ASML, Six crucial steps)

claim: Yield is the percentage of usable dies produced on a processed wafer.
evidence: "Yield refers to the percentage of usable die that are produced on a processed wafer." (Intel, Explaining Common Chip Terms)

claim: Intel defines a process node as the recipe and list of ingredients used in semiconductor fabrication.
evidence: "The recipe and list of ingredients used in semiconductor fabrication is called a process node." (Intel, Explaining Common Chip Terms)

claim: Process node names such as '7 nm' or '3 nm' no longer refer to any specific physical measurement on the chip, although historically they corresponded to transistor feature lengths.
evidence: "For decades, the process 'node' name corresponded to the actual length of certain physical transistor features"; "Today, the various naming and numbering schemes used across the industry no longer refer to any specific measurement and don't tell the full story" (Intel Accelerated fact sheet, July 2021, p. 3)

claim: Intel's Mark Bohr stated in 2013 that he could not point to any single dimension on a chip that equals the stated node name.
evidence: "I can't point to the one dimension that's 32 nm or 22 nm or 14 nm. Some dimensions are smaller than the stated node name, and others are larger." (IEEE Spectrum, Courtland, Oct 2013)

claim: 300 mm diameter wafers accounted for 99.7 percent of world fab capacity capable of manufacturing chips at 45 nm nodes or below.
evidence: "300 mm diameter wafers, which are used for 99.7 percent of the world's fab capacity capable of manufacturing chips at ≤45 nm nodes." (CSET, p. 57)

claim: In lithography, the circuit patterns from the design are mapped onto a glass plate called a photomask, and ultraviolet light transfers the pattern to photoresist on the wafer.
evidence: "The integrated circuit patterns specified in the design are mapped onto a glass plate called a photomask. An ultraviolet (UV) light is applied to transfer the patterns to the photoresist material coating on the wafer surface" (BCG/SIA 2021, p. 17)

claim: The smallest printable feature (critical dimension) follows the Rayleigh criterion CD = k1 x wavelength / NA, with a physical limit of k1 = 0.25.
evidence: "CD = k1 • λ / NA" ... k1 is "a coefficient that depends on many factors related to the chip manufacturing process. The physical limit lithography is k1 = 0.25" (ASML, The Rayleigh criterion)

claim: EUV lithography uses light with a wavelength of 13.5 nm.

claim: EUV light is generated by a CO2 laser firing two pulses at a fast-moving drop of tin, vaporizing it.

claim: Because EUV light is absorbed by everything including air, EUV systems use multilayer mirrors instead of lenses and keep the whole light path in high vacuum.
evidence: "EUV systems use several multilayer mirrors instead of lenses to guide the EUV light"; "EUV light is absorbed by everything, even air. So the whole light path ... must be in high vacuum" (ASML EUV page)

claim: ASML's NXE EUV systems have a numerical aperture of 0.33 and print features with a resolution of 13 nm.

claim: ASML's High-NA EXE EUV systems have a numerical aperture of 0.55 and print with a resolution of 8 nm.
evidence: EXE: "With an (NA) of 0.55"; "print with a resolution of just 8 nm" (ASML EUV page); "increased the NA from 0.33 in our NXE systems to 0.55 in EXE systems" (ASML, Jan 2024)

claim: High-NA EUV optics demagnify the mask pattern 4x in one direction and 8x in the other (anamorphic optics) to keep compatibility with existing reticles.
evidence: "demagnify it by 4x in one direction and 8x in the other" (ASML, 5 things you should know about High NA EUV, 25 Jan 2024)

claim: ASML shipped the first modules of the first High-NA EUV system to Intel in December 2023.
evidence: "ASML shipped the first modules of the first High NA EUV lithography system to Intel in December 2023" (ASML, 25 Jan 2024)

evidence: TSMC-Online offers "secure online business transactions and information transfer for product design, tape-outs, and wafer tracking," while TSMC-Direct provides "system-to-system integration service" (TSMC eFoundry page)

claim: The US DoD's DMEA accredits trusted suppliers in IC design, aggregation, brokering, mask manufacturing, foundry, post-processing, packaging/assembly and test.
evidence: "DMEA accredits suppliers in the areas of integrated circuit design, aggregation, broker, mask manufacturing, foundry, post processing, packaging/assembly and test services." (DMEA Trusted Supplier Program page)

claim: The DMEA Trusted Supplier Program aims to assure the integrity and confidentiality of integrated circuits during design and manufacturing, preventing tampering and unauthorized reverse engineering.
evidence: "assure the integrity and confidentiality of integrated circuits during design and manufacturing"; "Prevent intentional or unintentional modification or tampering of the ICs"; "Protect the ICs from unauthorized attempts at reverse engineering" (DMEA page)

claim: Experts consulted by GAO said semiconductor companies are hesitant to share information with each other, making actual demand for semiconductors difficult to determine.
evidence: "companies are hesitant to share information with each other and thus the actual demand for semiconductors is difficult to determine" (GAO-22-105923, p. 14)
notes: Expert opinion summarized by GAO, not a GAO finding.

claim: Experts consulted by GAO recommended a voluntary data-sharing mechanism improving visibility into second- to fourth-tier suppliers, without requiring disclosure of proprietary information.
evidence: "federal government should create and support a voluntary and timely data-sharing mechanism for firms that improves visibility into second, third and fourth tier suppliers"; "federal government should not require companies to disclose proprietary information when collecting and mapping supply chain data" (GAO-22-105923, p. 14)

claim: The US Commerce Department found that the median inventory of chips held by responding customers fell from 40 days in 2019 to less than five days during the 2021 shortage.
evidence: "The median inventory of chips has fallen from 40 days in 2019 to less than five days."; "More than 150 companies responded" (Commerce, 25 Jan 2022)

metric.name: Median chip inventory held by customers
metric.geography: United States (RFI respondents, global supply chains)
metric.population: Chip inventories reported by >150 RFI respondents

claim: In the 2021 shortage, legacy logic chips used in automobiles and medical devices faced the most acute shortages, and analog chips were in extremely high demand and short supply.
evidence: "Legacy logic chips used in automobiles, medical devices and other products are facing the most acute shortages."; "Analog chips used in power management, image sensors, radio frequency and other applications are in extremely high demand and short supply." (Commerce, 25 Jan 2022)

claim: The contractual terms governing access to leading-edge foundry PDKs (NDAs, licence scope, export-control screening) and how design data is protected in transit to foundries and mask shops are not publicly documented in the sources found.
evidence: Searched SkyWater/Google open PDK docs (which note open PDKs are unusual) and Synopsys glossary pages; TSMC eFoundry only states 'secure' transfer. No tier-1 document describing standard PDK licence/NDA terms was found.

claim: The number or share of mask layers exposed with EUV versus DUV at current leading-edge nodes could not be established from tier-1 sources in this pass.
evidence: ASML DUV page states DUV remains cost-effective for many layers, but no layer counts per node; ASML 2025 annual report excerpt gave no per-node EUV layer counts; web search budget exhausted before further searching.
